description:
Roaming Charges is five students from 3 countries running one Moon base across time zones. We are a group of first-year students from Babson College, ranked #1 in entrepreneurship by U.S. News, and the world renowned University of Southern California. 

Ray Kuang, USC / Irvine, California

King Oung, Babson College / London, UK 

Shubh Hosad, USC / Tennessee

Cyrus Lee, UCD

Warren Shao, USC

In space, you will only be able to communicate with mission control digitally. We’re already doing that.
summary: Mars Outpost is a co-op Roblox game where kids ages 7–12 keep a Martian base alive for 8 sols. Players run between machines to split limited solar power between Life Support (air and water), the Greenhouse (food), and Comms (science and storm warnings), while handling timed jobs and escalating disasters. Radiation storms are generated from real solar flares pulled live from NASA’s DONKI database, and resource values are grounded in NASA data such as Curiosity RAD radiation and ISS water recovery. Every choice has a cost, and a debrief links each player’s decisions to the outcome and to the real science, so players learn the actual trade-offs mission planners face. It runs on Roblox, a platform kids already use.
details:
What it does: Up to 6 players queue on a launch pad and are sent to a Mars outpost. They must keep Air, Water and Food above zero for 8 sols (Mars days), split into morning, noon, evening and night.

How it works:

  • Shared power trade-off: Solar output follows the day/night cycle; unused power charges a battery, and night has no sun. Players walk to a machine and press E/Q to add or remove power. Life Support needs more power at night for heaters; underpowered, air drops and water recovery falls from 98% to 93% (ISS figures). The Greenhouse needs 2 power to keep food steady. Comms produces science and is required to receive storm warnings from Earth, which arrive with a realistic 3–22 minute radio delay.
  • Safety vs. work: During radiation storms players must hide in a shielded shelter, where they cannot run machines or do jobs, so work piles up.
  • Jobs: Overcooked-style timed jobs (harvest crops, swap air filters, dig ice, collect rock samples, re-aim the dish) appear around the base and come faster as the mission goes on and with more players.
  • Escalating difficulty: Sols 1–2 are calm, then new problems are introduced one at a time: recycler failure, dust storm and dusty panels, two radiation storms (the second stronger), colder nights, and meteorite hull leaks. Event timing is randomized each round for replayability.
  • Learning by design: A picture-card tutorial, a “👉 Do this now” prompt, status labels on each machine, and disaster popups explaining what each event does and what to do keep it accessible for ages 7–12. The end-of-mission debrief shows the key decisions behind the outcome, trade-off lessons generated from that round, and real NASA facts with sources.
  • Collaboration: Work with other players to maintain resources and collaborate to fix issues like hull damage

Benefits: Kids experience the engineering trade-offs of a real outpost (power vs. safety vs. food vs. science) through play, not posters, on a platform they already use, with co-op play that encourages discussion.

Tools: Roblox Studio, Luau (server-authoritative simulation with validated client requests), Roblox HttpService (live NASA API calls), GitHub.

Goals: Add better 3D models (e.g., NASA 3D Resources), a Moon outpost mode, classroom mode, and localization.
